stories.headline: HOT SEPTEMBER CPI TRIGGERS S&P'S FIFTH LOSS IN SIX SESSIONS, NASDAQ'S WORST DAY SINCE JULY
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 1.11% to 7,718.94 and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to 26,692.87 — its sharpest one-day decline since July 23 — after a hotter-than-forecast September CPI report raised doubts the Fed can keep easing into year-end. AI-linked names led the slide, with CoreWeave plunging 15% on renewed debt-financing worries.
stories.explain: A CPI surprise doesn't just move the inflation headline — it instantly resets the market's model of the Fed's next several meetings, since traders price future rate paths into Fed funds futures in real time. That repricing raises the discount rate used to value future corporate cash flows, and the hit lands hardest on long-duration growth and AI names whose value sits mostly in earnings years away, which is exactly why chip and AI infrastructure stocks fell more than the broader index today.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD JUMPS TOWARD 5.3% AS HOT CPI FORCES A HAWKISH REPRICING
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 6 bps to roughly 5.28% and the 2-year jumped more than 10 bps to near 4.89% following the CPI print, extending a move that has already pushed 30-year mortgage rates toward 7.4%. The Fed hiked in September for the first time in three years, and its own projections imply one more quarter-point move by year-end — today's data makes markets more confident that happens.
stories.explain: The 2-year yield is the most sensitive to Fed-path expectations because it matures within the horizon of the next several meetings, so it jumped harder than the 10-year on today's news — a flattening move that signals the market sees the Fed staying restrictive for longer rather than growth expectations deteriorating. That's the mechanism directly behind the renewed pressure on mortgage rates and the discount-rate hit to equities in the same session.

stories.headline: OIL CLIMBS AS HOUTHI STRIKES ON SAUDI ARABIA AND IRAN'S HORMUZ THREATS COMPOUND THE INFLATION SHOCK
stories.body: Brent rose toward $106.60/bbl and WTI near $95 after Houthi forces struck targets inside Saudi Arabia and Iranian officials vowed to intensify tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic is already running roughly 30% below normal. Moody's estimates the eight-month-old U.S.-Iran conflict is now costing the average American household about $2,000 a year.
stories.explain: Oil is a direct line item in CPI through gasoline and heating costs, so today's twin shocks — a hot inflation print and a fresh supply threat at one of the world's most important chokepoints — reinforce each other: higher oil raises the odds of the next CPI report running hot too, which is exactly the feedback loop that makes energy-driven inflation so hard for a central bank to tame with interest rates alone.

stories.headline: BANK EARNINGS WEEK TURNS MIXED AS BOFA AND MORGAN STANLEY REPORT INTO A RATE SHOCK
stories.body: Citigroup ($2.85) and Wells Fargo ($1.87) topped profit estimates Tuesday while JPMorgan's $5.57 EPS missed the $5.93 consensus; Bank of America and Morgan Stanley reported Wednesday as the financial sector — down roughly 4% over the past month and about $270 billion in combined market value across the five majors — absorbs the fastest yield spike since September's hike.
stories.explain: Rising yields are a double-edged sword for banks: net interest margins widen as loan yields reprice faster than deposit costs, which flatters this quarter's trading and lending results, but a rate shock tied to an external inflation surprise also raises credit risk and recession odds, so the market is still deciding whether this week's results reflect a durable tailwind or a peak before the cycle turns.

stories.headline: FLORIDA TOPS PRESEASON TOP 25 AS MICHIGAN AND UCONN OPEN NEW ERAS WITH TIP-OFF THREE WEEKS AWAY
stories.body: With the Nov. 2 opener roughly three weeks out, ESPN's preseason Top 25 projects Florida at No. 1, while KenPom's model favors Duke. Reigning champion Michigan and runner-up UConn both enter the season under heavy roster turnover, and the AP's official preseason poll has not yet been released.

stories.headline: LAKERS' RECORD $12 BILLION SALE CLOSES AS LUKA DONCIC SITS OUT INDEFINITELY
stories.body: ESPN reports the Lakers' ownership sale has closed at a record $12 billion NBA valuation, even as the team opens the preseason without Luka Doncic — ruled out indefinitely by coach JJ Redick — and with LeBron James reportedly managing chronic arthritis. Elsewhere, Heat center Bam Adebayo exited a preseason game early with a lower-back injury, and the NBA Cup group-stage schedule kicks off Oct. 30 with the Lakers at the Warriors.

stories.headline: 49ERS STAY UNBEATEN AT 5-0; SEAHAWKS GET QUICK TURNAROUND AT BRONCOS THURSDAY
stories.body: San Francisco improved to 5-0 Sunday, rallying from a fourth-quarter deficit to beat Seattle 32-29 and drop the Seahawks to 3-2. Seattle gets a short week before visiting Denver for Thursday Night Football (8:15 p.m. ET), with both teams debuting throwback uniforms for the Week 6 showdown.

stories.headline: GEORGIA HOLDS NO. 1 IN AP POLL AS HUSKIES DROP TO 3-3 AHEAD OF FRIDAY AT PURDUE
stories.body: Georgia (6-0) remains No. 1 in this week's AP Top 25 with Notre Dame, Miami, Ohio State, and Indiana rounding out the top five, while Texas and Oregon continue to slide. Washington fell to 3-3 (0-3 Big Ten) in a blowout loss to Iowa and visits Purdue Friday, Oct. 16 — the Huskies' first trip to West Lafayette since 1990.

sports.detail: Split their first two preseason games: beat Phoenix 109-107, then fell in OT at Washington without Cade Cunningham or Jalen Duren. At Minnesota tonight, then host Toronto Oct. 16 before opening the regular season Oct. 20 vs. Boston.

deepDive.title: How One CPI Print Repriced the Entire Yield Curve in a Single Session
content: Today's brief has a tight common thread: a hotter-than-forecast September CPI report, a 10-year yield pushing toward 5.28%, a 2-year yield up over 10 bps to near 4.89%, and a Nasdaq having its worst day since July. None of those moved because new information arrived about the economy's long-run growth path — they moved because one data print changed what traders think the Federal Reserve will do at its next two or three meetings. That distinction matters for understanding why markets can swing so hard on a single release that, on its face, is just one month of price data.

The mechanism runs through Fed funds futures, a market where traders bet directly on the policy rate at future meeting dates. The moment CPI prints above consensus, that market repricing happens within seconds, before any Fed official says a word, because futures prices simply reflect the new probability distribution over future rate paths. Treasury yields then adjust to stay consistent with that repriced path: short-dated notes like the 2-year move most because they mature inside the window where the next few hikes would actually occur, while the 10-year moves less because it blends near-term policy with decades of long-run growth and inflation assumptions that one data point barely touches. That is exactly why the 2-year's 10+ bp move outpaced the 10-year's 6 bp move today.

What most people miss is that this is a flattening move, not a simple ‘rates up’ move — and flattening on a hawkish inflation surprise is a specific signal that the market expects the Fed to stay restrictive without conceding ground on long-run growth. The closest historical analogue is the string of 2022 CPI-day selloffs, when single above-consensus prints repeatedly produced 2%+ one-day drops in the S&P 500 as markets repriced a much steeper hiking path in real time; the September 2026 hike after three years on hold shows the Fed is explicitly trying to avoid repeating that era's slow, reactive policy path.

For today's setup specifically, the oil shock from Houthi strikes and Iran's Hormuz threats isn't a separate story from the CPI surprise — it's the channel that could keep feeding it. Energy costs run straight into next month's CPI basket, so a sustained supply shock raises the odds of another hot print, which would force Fed funds futures to reprice even further before the Fed's own meeting gets the chance to. That's why the single most important thing to watch isn't the next jobs report; it's whether oil holds its gains or a ceasefire headline unwinds the risk premium, because that outcome will likely determine whether today's yield spike is a one-day event or the start of a trend into the Fed's final two meetings of the year.
